option_description: Identifies the NFS protocol version actively used for a given mount or export (NFSv2, NFSv3, NFSv4.x). The version determines the available security mechanisms: NFSv2 and NFSv3 have no transport security options and transmit all data in cleartext, while NFSv4+ can be configured with Kerberos security flavors or TLS to provide authentication, integrity, and confidentiality.
security_impact: This is the primary determinant for multiple exposure rules. The Rego policy triggers 'cleartext_nfs_data_transmission' unconditionally for v2 and v3. It triggers 'rpc_replay_attack_exposure' for NFSv2/v3 because those versions have no RPCSEC_GSS sequence-number replay protection. 'in_transit_data_integrity_absence' and 'nfs_over_unencrypted_transport_layer' also fire immediately for v2/v3. NFSv4 without Kerberos (v4_no_krb) still triggers 'nfs_traffic_routing_manipulation' when traversing routed segments. Only v4_krb5p or v4_tls provide a path to clearing all high-severity transmission findings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS client, inspect active mount options using the mount command filtered to NFS entries. Look for vers= or nfsvers= in the options column.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'server:/export on /mnt/data type nfs4 (rw,vers=4.2,...)' or 'type nfs (rw,vers=3,...)' identifying the negotiated version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nfsstat on the client to display active NFS mount statistics including protocol version per mount point.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Per-mount output showing 'vers=3', 'vers=4', 'vers=4.1', or 'vers=4.2' alongside each mounted path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/fstab for static NFS mount entries. The vers= or nfsvers= option within the options field specifies the forced or preferred NFS version.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'server:/share /mnt nfs rw,vers=4.1,sec=krb5p 0 0' showing the configured version. Absence of vers= means the client and server negotiate the highest mutually supported version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, use nfsstat to view server-side statistics broken down by NFS version, revealing which protocol versions clients are actively using.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Statistics sections labeled 'Server nfs v3', 'Server nfs v4', etc., with non-zero call counts indicating active use of that version.

typical_values: v3 (extremely common in legacy deployments and default on many Linux distributions prior to RHEL 8)
v4_no_krb (common in environments that upgraded from v3 without adding Kerberos)
v4_krb5p (found in security-conscious enterprise environments with Active Directory or MIT Kerberos)
v4_tls (rare; requires kernel 5.15+ with in-kernel TLS and tlshd daemon)

option_description: Specifies the RPCSEC security flavor negotiated between NFS client and server via the sec= mount or export option. Controls what authentication, integrity, and confidentiality mechanisms are applied to RPC messages: 'sys' trusts client-asserted UIDs, 'auth_none' applies no authentication, 'krb5' adds mutual authentication, 'krb5i' adds per-message integrity MACs, 'krb5p' adds full RPC payload encryption, and 'tls' delegates security to the transport layer.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this value jointly with 'nfs_protocol_version' and 'nfs_tls_enabled' to evaluate 'cleartext_nfs_data_transmission': NFSv4 with sec=sys or sec=none and no TLS triggers the finding, as does sec=krb5 or sec=krb5i without TLS (data payload remains cleartext). 'rpc_replay_attack_exposure' fires when sec=sys or sec=none is used on NFSv4 because only RPCSEC_GSS provides sequence-number replay protection. The default value of 'sys' means the majority of unmodified deployments are exposed to these risks without explicit remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS client, inspect currently mounted NFS file systems and look for the sec= option in the mount options string.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output such as 'sys', 'krb5', 'krb5i', or 'krb5p'. Absence of sec= in the output implies the default 'sys' flavor is in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check /etc/fstab for the sec= option on NFS entries to determine what security flavor is statically configured for persistent mounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NFS mount lines; if sec= is absent the flavor defaults to 'sys'. Look for sec=krb5p as the most secure non-TLS option.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, inspect /etc/exports to determine which security flavors are permitted or required per export path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export lines such as '/data 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sec=krb5p)'. Missing sec= defaults to sys. The server-side sec= defines what the client may negotiate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nfsstat -m on the client to display the confirmed negotiated security flavor for each active mount.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mount details showing 'sec=krb5p' or 'sec=sys' confirming the active negotiated flavor.

typical_values: sys (default in the vast majority of Linux NFS deployments; represents the insecure baseline)
krb5 (deployed in environments with Kerberos infrastructure but without integrity requirements)
krb5i (used when data tampering detection is required without full payload encryption overhead)
krb5p (used in high-security environments; adds encryption overhead but fully secures the RPC layer)
auth_none (rare, seen only in intentionally open or diagnostic configurations)

option_description: Indicates whether NFS traffic is protected by TLS at the transport layer using the xprtsec=tls or xprtsec=mtls mount options, implementing RFC 9289 (NFS-over-TLS). When enabled, all NFS traffic including RPC headers, data payloads, and Kerberos ticket exchanges is wrapped in TLS, providing transport-level confidentiality and integrity independent of the RPCSEC security flavor.
security_impact: This boolean directly gates multiple high-severity Rego findings. 'cleartext_nfs_data_transmission' fires for NFSv4 with sec=sys, sec=none, sec=krb5, or sec=krb5i *only when nfs_tls_enabled is false*, because TLS independently encrypts the transport. 'in_transit_data_integrity_absence' fires for NFSv4 when both rpcsec_gss_integrity_enabled and nfs_tls_enabled are false. 'nfs_over_unencrypted_transport_layer' fires for v4.1/v4.2 when nfs_tls_enabled is false and no security flavor is set. Critically, 'kerberos_ticket_interception_in_transit' fires whenever rpcsec_gss_enabled is true but nfs_tls_enabled is false, because Kerberos ticket exchanges are exposed to capture and Kerberoasting without transport encryption.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check current NFS mounts for the xprtsec= option which indicates NFS-over-TLS configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'xprtsec=tls' or 'xprtsec=mtls' confirms TLS is active. No output or absent xprtsec= means TLS is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the kernel TLS module and the tlshd (or rpc.tlsd) userspace daemon are loaded and running, which are prerequisites for NFS-over-TLS.
how_to_obtain.command: lsmod | grep '^tls' && systemctl is-active tlshd 2>/dev/null || systemctl is-active rpc-tlsd 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: First command outputs 'tls' module entry. Second outputs 'active'. Both must be true for NFS-over-TLS to function.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, check /etc/nfs.conf for the tls=yes directive under the [nfsd] section which enables server-side NFS-over-TLS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'tls=yes' indicates server-side TLS is enabled. Absence or 'tls=no' indicates it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for NFS TLS certificates installed on the system, which are required for TLS mutual authentication (xprtsec=mtls).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificate and key files (cert.pem, key.pem, ca.pem or similar) present in the NFS TLS certificate directory. Absence confirms TLS is not configured.

typical_values: false (default and nearly universal; NFS-over-TLS requires kernel 5.15+, tlshd, and PKI infrastructure that most environments lack)
true (found only in bleeding-edge Linux deployments, typically RHEL 9.3+/Fedora with explicit hardening; rare in production)

option_description: Indicates whether RPCSEC_GSS with Kerberos authentication is configured for this NFS mount or export (sec=krb5, sec=krb5i, or sec=krb5p). RPCSEC_GSS provides cryptographically verified mutual authentication between client and server using Kerberos tickets, and its sequence-number mechanism provides replay attack protection that is absent in AUTH_SYS.
security_impact: This boolean is central to 'rpc_replay_attack_exposure': the Rego policy fires this finding for NFSv4 whenever rpcsec_gss_enabled is false, because only RPCSEC_GSS provides sequence-number-based replay protection. It also gates 'kerberos_ticket_interception_in_transit': this finding fires when rpcsec_gss_enabled is true but nfs_tls_enabled is false, because Kerberos ticket exchanges over an unencrypted transport can be captured for offline cracking or replay. The combination of rpcsec_gss_enabled=false and nfs_tls_enabled=false represents the worst-case configuration for NFSv4 transit security.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check active NFS mounts for Kerberos security flavors in the sec= option, which indicates RPCSEC_GSS is in use.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing 'sec=krb5', 'sec=krb5i', or 'sec=krb5p' confirm RPCSEC_GSS is active. No matching output means RPCSEC_GSS is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the rpc-gssd or gssproxy service is running, which is required for RPCSEC_GSS operation on the client side.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of 1 or 2 indicates at least one GSS daemon is active. A count of 0 means RPCSEC_GSS is non-functional regardless of mount options.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/fstab for NFS entries with sec= options containing a krb5 variant, indicating RPCSEC_GSS is configured for persistent mounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching lines show Kerberos-protected mounts are persistently configured. No output means RPCSEC_GSS is not configured in static mounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, check /etc/exports for sec=krb5 variants on export entries to confirm server-side RPCSEC_GSS requirement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export entries containing 'sec=krb5', 'sec=krb5i', or 'sec=krb5p'. Absence means the server allows or defaults to AUTH_SYS.

typical_values: false (dominant default; most NFS deployments use AUTH_SYS and have never configured Kerberos infrastructure)
true (found in enterprise environments with Active Directory integration or dedicated MIT Kerberos KDC, particularly in finance and healthcare sectors)

option_description: Indicates whether RPCSEC_GSS integrity protection is configured via sec=krb5i or sec=krb5p. These flavors add per-message Message Integrity Codes (MICs) to every RPC operation, enabling detection of in-transit tampering of file data, metadata, and RPC responses. krb5i provides integrity without encryption; krb5p provides both integrity and full RPC payload encryption.
security_impact: This boolean directly controls the 'in_transit_data_integrity_absence' finding: the Rego policy fires this for NFSv4 when both rpcsec_gss_integrity_enabled and nfs_tls_enabled are false, meaning neither RPC-layer MICs nor transport TLS are providing integrity verification. Without integrity protection, a MITM attacker can silently modify NFS read responses (corrupting files received by the client) or forge write acknowledgements. Note that sec=krb5 alone (authentication only, without integrity) does not set this to true—only krb5i or krb5p qualify.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check active NFS mounts specifically for sec=krb5i or sec=krb5p, which are the only flavors that enable RPCSEC_GSS integrity protection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing 'sec=krb5i' or 'sec=krb5p' confirm integrity protection is active. 'sec=krb5' alone does not provide integrity and should not be treated as a match.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/fstab NFS entries for sec=krb5i or sec=krb5p to determine if integrity is configured for persistent mounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching entries confirm integrity-protected persistent mounts are configured. Entries with sec=krb5 only (no trailing i or p) do not provide integrity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, verify that exports are configured with sec=krb5i or sec=krb5p to enforce integrity protection server-side.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export entries containing sec=krb5i or sec=krb5p. Note that listing multiple flavors (e.g., sec=sys:krb5:krb5i:krb5p) allows downgrade negotiation—only entries where krb5i or krb5p is the sole or required option enforce integrity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nfsstat -m to confirm the active negotiated security flavor includes integrity (krb5i or krb5p) for each mount.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mount statistics entries showing sec=krb5i or sec=krb5p as the active negotiated flavor, confirming integrity is operationally enforced.

typical_values: false (default; even environments that have deployed Kerberos for NFS frequently stop at sec=krb5 for authentication only, not upgrading to krb5i or krb5p due to performance concerns)
true (found in security-mature enterprises, particularly where compliance frameworks such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or FedRAMP require data integrity in transit)

option_description: Indicates whether the full Kerberos operational stack required for RPCSEC_GSS is properly configured and functional. All three conditions must be simultaneously true: (1) a keytab file exists containing a valid nfs/ service principal, (2) the rpc.gssd or gssproxy daemon is running and able to read the keytab, and (3) the KDC is network-reachable from both the NFS client and server. A partially configured Kerberos setup results in mount failures or fallback to AUTH_SYS.
security_impact: This attribute gates the 'missing_mutual_authentication_on_mount' finding for the case where Kerberos is apparently configured (auth_flavor is krb5/krb5i/krb5p) but the infrastructure is non-functional. The Rego policy fires this finding when auth_flavor is a Kerberos variant but kerberos_configured is false—this catches the dangerous scenario where an administrator has set sec=krb5p in /etc/fstab but the underlying infrastructure has degraded (expired keytab, stopped gssd, KDC unreachable), potentially causing clients to fail secure mounts or mount with reduced security.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the NFS service principal keytab exists and contains a valid nfs/ principal entry, which is required for RPCSEC_GSS to function.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as '1 nfs/server.example.com@REALM' confirming the NFS service principal is present in the keytab. Absence means Kerberos authentication will fail.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the GSS authentication daemon (rpc-gssd or gssproxy) is active and running, which is the userspace component that processes Kerberos ticket exchanges for NFS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Active: active (running)' for either rpc-gssd or gssproxy. Both stopped indicates RPCSEC_GSS operations will fail silently or cause mount errors.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test KDC reachability from the NFS client and server by attempting to obtain a Kerberos ticket, which verifies the KDC is reachable and the principal is valid.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful kinit with 'Credentials cache' output and a valid expiry time. Errors such as 'Cannot contact any KDC' or 'Key table entry not found' indicate infrastructure failures.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review /etc/krb5.conf to verify KDC realm configuration is present and points to reachable KDC hosts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'kdc = kdc.example.com' under the configured realm. Missing or placeholder entries indicate Kerberos infrastructure is not properly configured.

typical_values: false (most common; Kerberos for NFS requires deliberate infrastructure setup that the majority of organizations have not implemented)
true (found in Active Directory-integrated Linux environments using SSSD/winbind, or purpose-built Kerberos-secured NFS deployments in regulated industries)

option_description: Specifies the RPC authentication mechanism negotiated for the NFS session at the RPC layer (distinct from but related to nfs_security_flavor). AUTH_SYS (also called AUTH_UNIX) is the default and trusts client-asserted UID/GID values with no cryptographic verification whatsoever—any client that can reach the NFS port can claim any user identity. AUTH_NONE provides zero authentication. The Kerberos variants (krb5, krb5i, krb5p) use RPCSEC_GSS for cryptographically verified mutual authentication.
security_impact: This attribute directly drives 'missing_mutual_authentication_on_mount': the Rego policy fires this finding for NFSv4 when auth_flavor is auth_sys or auth_none, because neither provides server-to-client or client-to-server identity verification. A client using AUTH_SYS can impersonate any UID (including root if no_root_squash is set on the server) simply by setting the effective UID before making NFS calls. The finding also fires when auth_flavor is a Kerberos variant but kerberos_configured is false, catching degraded-configuration scenarios. AUTH_NONE is particularly dangerous as it bypasses all access controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect active NFS mounts for the sec= parameter which directly maps to the auth_flavor in use. The absence of sec= implies auth_sys.
how_to_obtain.command:
mount | grep -i nfs | awk -F'(' '{print $2}' | tr ',' '
' | grep -E '^sec='
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like 'sec=sys', 'sec=krb5', 'sec=krb5i', 'sec=krb5p'. No sec= line means AUTH_SYS is active by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check /etc/fstab NFS mount entries for the sec= option to determine the statically configured authentication flavor.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NFS fstab entries with line numbers. Examine the options field (4th column) for sec=; absence defaults to auth_sys which should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the NFS server, inspect /etc/exports to determine which authentication flavors are permitted or enforced for each exported path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export entries; look for sec= in export options. 'sec=sys:krb5p' allows downgrade to sys; 'sec=krb5p' only enforces Kerberos privacy. No sec= defaults to sys.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use rpcinfo to query what authentication flavors the NFS server advertises as supported, which shows what the server will negotiate.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RPC service listings for NFS programs. Combined with /etc/exports inspection, this confirms what the server accepts. Primarily used to verify NFS service is listening.

typical_values: auth_sys (dominant default; present on nearly all unmodified NFS deployments across Linux, BSD, and Solaris)
krb5p (found in hardened enterprise environments with full Kerberos infrastructure and compliance requirements)
krb5i (used as a performance compromise—integrity without encryption overhead—in environments where confidentiality is addressed by other controls)
auth_none (rare; typically only in intentionally public exports or broken configurations)

option_description: Specifies the list of Kerberos encryption types that are permitted or negotiated in the KDC and client/server configuration for this NFS deployment. This array determines the cryptographic strength of Kerberos tickets and session keys exchanged during RPCSEC_GSS authentication. Weak types such as rc4-hmac (RC4 with HMAC-MD5), des-cbc-md5, and des3-cbc-sha1 are vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks and Kerberoasting. Strong types include aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 and aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192.
security_impact: This array is evaluated by 'kerberos_ticket_interception_in_transit': the Rego policy fires this finding when rpcsec_gss_enabled is true, nfs_tls_enabled is false, and rc4-hmac appears in kerberos_encryption_types. When Kerberos tickets are transmitted without TLS and use weak encryption types, an attacker who captures the ticket can perform offline Kerberoasting (for service tickets) or AS-REP roasting (for user tickets) to recover the underlying password or key. Even without cracking, captured RC4-encrypted tickets may be replayable in some configurations. The use of modern AES encryption types significantly raises the cost of offline attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/krb5.conf on both NFS client and server for the default_tkt_enctypes and default_tgs_enctypes directives under [libdefaults], which define permitted encryption types for ticket requests and service tickets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'default_tkt_enctypes = aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96'. Presence of 'rc4-hmac', 'des-cbc-md5', or 'des3-cbc-sha1' indicates weak types are permitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the Kerberos KDC server, inspect kdc.conf for the supported_enctypes directive which controls what encryption types the KDC will use when issuing tickets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'supported_enctypes = aes256-cts:normal aes128-cts:normal' (secure). Presence of 'arcfour-hmac:normal' or 'des3-hmac-sha1:normal' indicates weak types are enabled at the KDC.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Obtain an actual NFS service ticket and inspect the encryption type used, which reveals what was negotiated in practice between this client and KDC.
how_to_obtain.command: kinit $(whoami) && kvno nfs/$(grep -m1 nfs /etc/fstab | awk '{print $1}' | cut -d: -f1) && klist -e | grep -A2 'nfs/'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'Etype (skey, tkt): aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96, ...' for a secure configuration. 'arcfour-hmac' or 'rc4-hmac' in the etype line indicates weak encryption was negotiated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use klist with the -e flag on an existing credentials cache to display the encryption types of current tickets, revealing what types were negotiated in the most recent authentication.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'Etype (skey, tkt): aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96, aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96' for strong configuration. RC4 or DES entries indicate vulnerable encryption types are in use.

typical_values: ['aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96', 'aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96'] (modern secure default on RHEL 8+/Debian 11+)
['aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96', 'aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96', 'rc4-hmac'] (common in hybrid Windows/Linux environments with legacy AD compatibility requirements)
['rc4-hmac', 'des3-cbc-sha1', 'des-cbc-md5'] (legacy configurations, particularly those with Windows Server 2003-era or older Samba-based KDCs)
['aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192', 'aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128'] (RFC 8009 modern types, found only in very recent RHEL 9/Ubuntu 22.04+ deployments with explicit hardening)

option_description: Controls whether rpcbind/portmapper (port 111 TCP/UDP) is reachable from untrusted or external network segments. rpcbind acts as the NFS port broker; exposure allows attackers to intercept or spoof port assignments, redirecting NFS clients to rogue servers.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires portmapper_rpcbind_interception when rpcbind_network_exposure is 'internet_exposed' or 'untrusted_network' AND portmapper_response_authentication_enabled is false. Wide exposure transforms rpcbind into an unauthenticated pivot point enabling NFS session hijacking and denial-of-service via invalid port responses.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check iptables/nftables rules on the NFS server for port 111 access restrictions
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep ':111' && nft list ruleset | grep 111
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules restricting port 111 to specific source IPs/subnets; absence of rules permitting 0.0.0.0/0

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test port 111 reachability from an external or untrusted host to confirm firewall enforcement
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Port 111 should show 'filtered' or 'closed' from untrusted sources; 'open' indicates exposure

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud or on-premises firewall/ACL rules for port 111 policies on the NFS server's network interface
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Port 111 bound only to internal interfaces; firewall zones showing restricted source access

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect hosts.allow and hosts.deny TCP wrappers configuration that may restrict rpcbind access
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'rpcbind: 10.0.1.0/24' in hosts.allow and 'rpcbind: ALL' in hosts.deny confirm restriction

typical_values: internal_only (most common in properly hardened environments)
untrusted_network (common in flat enterprise networks lacking micro-segmentation)
internet_exposed (rare but observed in misconfigured cloud VMs with overly permissive security groups)
blocked (best practice when static NFS ports bypass portmapper)

option_description: Indicates whether rpcbind/portmapper responses are cryptographically authenticated or whether static NFS port configuration bypasses portmapper entirely. Without this, clients blindly trust any portmapper response, making them vulnerable to spoofed port assignments.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers portmapper_rpcbind_interception when rpcbind is exposed to internet or untrusted networks AND this attribute is false. Since default rpcbind implementations offer no RPCSEC_GSS-level response authentication, spoofed responses can silently redirect all NFS mounts to attacker-controlled servers, enabling full data interception.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check nfs.conf and rpcbind configuration for static port assignments that bypass portmapper lookups
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'port=2049' under [nfsd] section indicate static ports; absence means portmapper is consulted

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify if NFS daemons are bound to static ports rather than dynamically registered with rpcbind
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Static port assignments (e.g., mountd always on 20048) suggest portmapper bypass; dynamic random ports indicate portmapper dependency

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check NFS server service configuration for fixed mountd and lockd port settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Variables like RPCMOUNTDOPTS='--port 20048' or STATDOPTS='--port 32765' indicate static assignment

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview NFS administrators to determine if RPCSEC_GSS is deployed at the portmapper level or if network controls substitute for authentication
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation of either RPCSEC_GSS usage at portmapper level (rare) or documented static port configuration policy

typical_values: false (nearly universal default; rpcbind has no built-in response authentication)
true (only when static ports fully bypass portmapper or RPCSEC_GSS is explicitly deployed at portmapper level)

option_description: Determines whether NFS traffic crosses Layer 3 routing boundaries including inter-VLAN routing, WAN links, or routed campus networks, rather than staying within a single flat Layer 2 segment. Routed traversal expands the attack surface for traffic manipulation.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires nfs_traffic_routing_manipulation when nfs_traverses_routed_segments is true and the NFS version lacks Kerberos, or when Kerberos is used but ICMP redirects are not disabled. Routing boundaries introduce BGP hijacking, ARP spoofing at gateway interfaces, and ICMP redirect injection vectors that can silently reroute NFS streams.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run traceroute from NFS client to NFS server to count routing hops; more than one hop through a router confirms routed traversal
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Single hop (direct L2) = false; multiple hops through router IPs = true

how_to_obtain.instruction: Compare NFS client and server IP addresses and subnet masks to determine if they share the same L2 subnet
how_to_obtain.command: ip route get <nfs-server-ip> && ip addr show && arp -n <nfs-server-ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 'ip route get' shows 'via <gateway-ip>', traffic is routed (true); if it shows 'dev <iface> src' with no via, it is L2-local (false)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ping with TTL=1 to verify whether NFS server is on the same L2 segment
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TTL exceeded response from a router confirms routed path; direct reply indicates L2-local

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network topology diagrams and VLAN configuration to determine if NFS server and clients are in different subnets or VLANs requiring L3 routing
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Network diagram showing NFS client/server in separate VLANs with routing between them confirms true

typical_values: false (ideal; NFS on dedicated storage VLAN with clients co-located)
true (common in large enterprises where storage is centralized and clients span multiple VLANs)

option_description: Controls whether NFS client and server hosts accept ICMP redirect messages (Type 5), which can be used to poison routing tables and silently reroute NFS traffic through attacker-controlled hosts performing man-in-the-middle attacks.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes icmp_redirects_disabled as a mitigating condition: when nfs_traverses_routed_segments is true and NFS uses Kerberos (krb5/krb5i), if ICMP redirects are NOT disabled the routing manipulation finding still fires. ICMP redirect injection is a low-complexity attack on routed segments that defeats Kerberos authentication by replacing the legitimate server in the routing path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check kernel sysctl parameters for ICMP redirect acceptance on both NFS client and server hosts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All values should be 0; any value of 1 means ICMP redirects are accepted (insecure)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify persistent sysctl configuration to ensure ICMP redirect settings survive reboots
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0' and 'net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0' present

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check all network interface-specific ICMP redirect settings to catch per-interface overrides
how_to_obtain.command: for iface in $(ls /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/); do echo "$iface: $(cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/$iface/accept_redirects)"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All interfaces (including specific NFS-facing interfaces) should show 0

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows NFS hosts, check registry and firewall rules blocking ICMP Type 5 redirects
how_to_obtain.command: reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters /v EnableICMPRedirect && netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=all | findstr ICMP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: EnableICMPRedirect = 0x0 or firewall rule blocking ICMP type 5 confirms protection

typical_values: true (correctly hardened Linux servers following CIS benchmarks)
false (default on many Linux distributions; requires explicit hardening)
null (not assessed or mixed client/server state)

option_description: Indicates whether per-client bandwidth or rate limiting controls are configured at the NFS server or nearby network devices to prevent any single NFS client from saturating the shared network link with high-volume read/write operations.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires absence_of_nfs_traffic_rate_limiting when BOTH nfs_client_bandwidth_limit_configured AND nfs_network_qos_policy_applied are false. Without rate limiting, a single misconfigured or compromised NFS client can generate read/write storms that deny NFS service to all other consumers sharing the storage path, representing a protocol-level denial of service vector.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect NFS export configuration for any bandwidth-limiting export options on the NFS server
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export options like 'rw,sync,no_root_squash,bwlimit=100000' would indicate bandwidth controls; most deployments lack these options

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check NFS server daemon configuration for rate limiting or throttling parameters
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of rate/limit parameters confirms controls; most nfs.conf files have no such parameters

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check storage appliance or NFS gateway for per-share or per-client throughput limits via CLI
how_to_obtain.command: nfs export show -fields max-read-size,max-write-size 2>/dev/null || zfs get quota,recordsize <pool/dataset> 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ZFS or NetApp/EMC quota and throughput limits confirm server-side controls exist

how_to_obtain.instruction: For enterprise NAS appliances (NetApp ONTAP, EMC Isilon, TrueNAS), review per-share QoS and throughput policies in the storage management console
how_to_obtain.navigation: NetApp ONTAP: System Manager > Storage > Volumes > QoS Policy | TrueNAS: Storage > Pools > Edit Dataset > Advanced Options > Bandwidth
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Named QoS policy with maximum throughput limits assigned to NFS shares confirms bandwidth limiting

typical_values: false (default and most common; NFS protocol has no native bandwidth controls)
true (enterprise NAS environments using storage QoS policies or network traffic shapers)

option_description: Determines whether a network-level Quality of Service or traffic shaping policy enforces bandwidth limits on the NFS transport path at the switch, router, or SDN fabric level, preventing bandwidth monopolization by individual NFS clients.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires absence_of_nfs_traffic_rate_limiting when both nfs_network_qos_policy_applied and nfs_client_bandwidth_limit_configured are false. Network QoS at the switch/router level is the compensating control when the NFS server lacks per-client throttling. Without either control, link saturation attacks require only legitimate NFS credentials and a fast client.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Linux traffic control (tc) policies on the NFS network interface for bandwidth policers targeting NFS traffic (TCP 2049)
how_to_obtain.command: tc qdisc show dev <nfs-interface> && tc filter show dev <nfs-interface> | grep -A5 '2049'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTB or TBF qdiscs with filters matching TCP port 2049 and rate limits confirm QoS enforcement

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review switch/router QoS configuration on the port or VLAN carrying NFS traffic for bandwidth policers
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco IOS: show policy-map interface <int> | Juniper: show class-of-service interface <int> | Aruba/HP: show qos port-policy <port>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy-map with police action targeting NFS DSCP markings or TCP 2049 flows confirms enforcement

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify DSCP markings on NFS traffic and check if enforcement policies (not just marking) are in place on network devices
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i <nfs-interface> -c 100 tcp port 2049 -v 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'tos|dscp' | sort | uniq -c
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Consistent DSCP values suggest QoS marking; enforcement must be verified on the network device separately

how_to_obtain.instruction: Consult network operations team or review SDN fabric documentation for per-flow bandwidth policies on the storage network segment
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented QoS policy referencing NFS ports (2049) with enforced bandwidth limits on the storage VLAN confirms the control

typical_values: false (most common; many organizations do not apply granular QoS to internal storage VLANs)
true (enterprise environments with dedicated storage fabrics and SDN-managed bandwidth policies)
